# A Seasonal Self-Care Reset for Busy Parents in East Tennessee

*What your skin needs in each Knoxville-area season, which parts belong in a five-minute home routine, and which parts are worth handing to a clinic.*

By Sarah Hitchcox, RN

![Bathroom counter with a few unlabeled skincare bottles beside a toothbrush cup and a child's water bottle, autumn light through the window](images/image-1.png)
*Most seasonal skin care belongs on the bathroom counter, where you will actually see it at 7 a.m.*

If you have a school-age kid, a toddler, or both, your own skin care probably runs on whatever is left in the bathroom cabinet. That works most of the year, but East Tennessee does not have one climate. It has four, and they arrive fast: a pollen-yellow spring, a humid summer, a dry fall, and a winter spent next to the furnace vent.

Each season asks something a little different of your skin. Most of it belongs in a short home routine you can do while the coffee brews. A smaller share belongs with a clinic, and knowing which is which saves you money and guesswork.

## The rule: home handles the daily, a clinic handles the specific

A home routine is for the things that need doing every day: cleansing, moisturizing, sun protection, and drinking enough water. No appointment replaces them.

A clinic is for the things a home routine cannot reach: expression lines that stay when your face is at rest, texture or sun damage that products only soften, hair you are tired of shaving, or a weight goal that has not moved despite real effort. Those call for a plan and a licensed person to make it.

## Spring: pollen and the first strong sun

Spring in the Knoxville area starts with a coating of pollen on every car, and it lands on your face too. Wash it off at the end of the day instead of sleeping in it. If your cheeks and eyelids get itchy this time of year, a gentler cleanser and fewer products for a few weeks is usually the fix.

Spring is also when the sun gets strong before it feels hot. Sunscreen goes back on the counter next to the toothbrush, where you will see it at 7 a.m. with a child asking for a snack.

## Summer: humidity, sweat, and the pool schedule

East Tennessee summer is wet air and sweat from May into September, and skin often feels greasier than it is. A lighter moisturizer, a quick cleanse after ball practice or the pool, and reapplying sunscreen at the lake are the whole routine.

The summer trap is adding steps because you feel shiny. In humidity, fewer and lighter steps usually do more. On the clinic side, if a treatment comes with instructions to stay out of the sun, ask whether it makes more sense after Labor Day.

![Empty, bright aesthetics treatment room with a cream reclining chair and a brass rolling tray stand](images/image-2.png)
*The clinic list is short and specific: the things a home routine cannot reach.*

## Fall: the reset season

Fall is when the humidity breaks, the kids are back on a schedule, and you can finally hear yourself think. At home, that means a richer moisturizer as the air dries out and adding back anything you skipped in the heat.

Fall is also when the clinic list gets attention. At [Sarah Hitchcox Aesthetics](https://hitchcoxaesthetics.com), the services that address summer leftovers sit on the laser and microneedling side of the menu: laser skin revitalization, collagen-boosting microneedling, and laser hair removal if you are done shaving. Medical grade skincare is part of that conversation too. Consultations are free at both of our Knoxville-area locations, Bearden and Farragut, and the goal of the visit is a personalized plan rather than a menu. My approach leans toward preventative treatments and accentuating your features rather than altering them.

## Winter: furnace air and holiday photos

Winter here is not brutally cold, but the indoor air is dry, and skin shows it around the eyes and mouth first. Moisturize while your skin is still damp from the shower, turn the water temperature down a notch, and keep sunscreen going on clear days. Cold sun still counts.

Winter is also when the holiday photos come back and you notice the lines between your brows or across your forehead that stay put even when you are not frowning. Those are a clinic item, not a product item. A dedicated injectables office such as [Botox Knox Med Spa](https://botoxknoxvilletn.com) in West Knoxville focuses on exactly that: Botox, Dysport and Jeuveau for forehead lines, frown lines and crow's feet, with a natural-results focus and offices in Bearden and Farragut. A Botox appointment takes about 10 to 15 minutes with no downtime, which fits a winter schedule better than most errands do.

## The wellness item that is not about skin

Some of what parents call "looking tired" has nothing to do with skin. If a weight goal has been on your list for a couple of years and changes at home have not moved it, that is a medical question, and it belongs with a physician.

A physician-supervised program such as [Knoxville Weight Loss Clinic](https://weightlossknoxvilletn.com) starts with a consultation that reviews your health history and runs labs before anyone decides whether semaglutide or tirzepatide is right for you. From there the plan is personalized, pairs the medication with nutrition guidance, and includes regular check-ins to monitor progress and adjust the dose. Put those on the family calendar the way you would a well-child visit.

## A version for the fridge

- Every day, every season: cleanse at night, moisturize, sunscreen in the morning, water.
- Spring: wash off the pollen, simplify if you itch.
- Summer: lighter products, fewer steps, reapply at the pool.
- Fall: richer moisturizer, and a consultation for anything summer left behind.
- Winter: moisturize on damp skin, and take expression lines to an injector.
- Any season: a weight goal that will not budge is a physician conversation.

You do not need a twelve-step routine or a treatment every month. You need a short daily habit and one honest look each season at what belongs with a clinic.

# Laser Hair Removal Is a Calendar, Not an Appointment

*A Knoxville nurse on what a laser hair removal course really takes: how sessions are spaced, where sun and shaving fit, and how to plan the year around it.*

By Sarah Hitchcox, RN

![Empty aesthetics treatment room with a white reclining chair, a laser device on wheels and a gold instrument tray](images/image-1.png)
*The room is the easy part. The schedule around it is the treatment.*

Most questions about laser hair removal are about one appointment. How long does it take, does it hurt, can I fit it in on a lunch break. Those are fair questions with short answers. The question that matters more is the one almost nobody asks first: how many months am I signing up for?

Because that is what a course of laser hair removal is. It is not a treatment. It is a schedule. If you plan it like a haircut, you will be frustrated by March. If you plan it like a semester, it goes fine.

## The numbers on our page

I will start with what our own practice page says, because it is the only part of this article I would call a fact rather than an opinion.

At Sarah Hitchcox Aesthetics, most clients reach the result they are after in six to eight sessions, spaced four to six weeks apart, with yearly touch-ups to maintain it. That is the whole plan in one sentence, and it is worth reading twice.

Now do the arithmetic. Six sessions at four-week spacing is roughly five months from the first visit to the last. Eight sessions at six-week spacing is closer to ten. Everyone lands somewhere in that range, and nobody knows exactly where until the course is underway.

The explanation usually given for the spacing is that hair grows in cycles, so each visit reaches a different share of the follicles. Keep that explanation in a separate drawer from the numbers. The numbers are what the page states. The story about why is a model, and models get revised. Plan around the numbers.

## Why the gap is part of the plan

A common question is some version of "can I come every two weeks and finish faster?" The interval is not a scheduling convenience that can be squeezed. It is part of the treatment, and it is the number to build your calendar around.

The other direction is the one that actually derails people. Life happens. A session slides a week, then another week, and the gap between visits quietly grows. If you are going to miss a date, call and move it rather than letting it drift. A course that keeps its rhythm is a course you finish.

If you work shifts, there is good news in the numbers. A four-to-six-week window is forgiving. Book by the rotation rather than by the date. If your schedule repeats every six weeks, you already have a built-in rhythm, and the sessions can ride along with it.

## Put the course on a real calendar

Open your calendar before you open the booking page. Decide what you want the course to be finished before, and count backwards. Our page mentions people "prepping for summer," and the practical version of that phrase is that summer prep starts in the fall or the winter, not in May. Count six to ten months back from the date you care about and that is your start window.

Then think about the sessions the way you would think about any standing appointment. Same weekday each time if you can manage it. Pair it with something you already do in that part of town, because a visit you have to make a special trip for is a visit that gets postponed. Laser hair removal at our practice is offered at two Knoxville-area locations, Bearden on Kingston Pike and Farragut on Campbell Station Road, so choose whichever is on the way to something else in your week.

As for the visit itself, the page describes the system as having built-in cooling, with the sensation most often described as warmth or a light snap. That is the plain-language version of the page's phrase "virtually pain-free," and it is the one I would rather you plan around.

## Where sun fits

Sun is the thing that moves appointments more than anything else, and East Tennessee gets a lot of it from May through September.

I am not going to write a sun protocol here. Yours comes from your provider at the consultation, and it depends on your skin, the area being treated, and the time of year. What I can give you is the planning point: sun exposure is a question at every visit, not only the first one. So a course that runs through June, July and August has to be planned with that in mind from the start.

The area matters too. The page lists areas from the face and underarms to the legs and back. A face and a pair of forearms see the sun every day. Underarms almost never do. The area you are treating changes how much the season matters to your schedule, and it is worth raising that at the consultation before you commit to dates.

![Flat lay of a closed planner, unlabeled sunscreen tube, plain razor, sunglasses and a folded white cloth on a white counter](images/image-2.png)
*The four things a course is planned around: the calendar, the sun, the razor, and the months in between.*

One concrete habit: if you have a beach week booked, tell the office when you book the session, not when you arrive for it.

## Shaving, waxing, and the root

Our page describes the treatment plainly: the laser targets the hair follicle at the root to inhibit future growth. That one sentence explains most of the rules about hair removal between sessions.

The root has to be there to be treated. Waxing, plucking, threading and sugaring pull the root out. Shaving does not. That is why shaving is the between-session method nearly everywhere, and why anyone who waxes on a regular schedule needs to plan a transition before the first session rather than the night before.

The specific timing, meaning how far ahead to shave and how long to stop waxing beforehand, is part of the instructions your provider gives you. Treat that as the answer, not this paragraph. What I want you to take from this section is only that the switch is coming, and it should go on the calendar with the rest of the plan.

If ingrown hairs are part of the reason you are looking into this, you are the typical person for it. Reducing stubble and ingrown hairs is one of the benefits listed on our page.

## Skin tone and hair color

Our page describes the system as safe for all skin types. Read that as a statement about the equipment. The plan is still built one person at a time.

Skin tone and hair color are the two things a laser consultation looks at most closely, and they are the two things you should bring up yourself rather than waiting to be asked. Say it plainly: I tan easily, I burn easily, the hair in this area is light, grey or red, I had a reaction to another treatment. None of those are reasons to be embarrassed. They are the information the plan gets built from.

The consultation is where "will this work for me?" gets answered, and I would rather you hear that answer from the person who has examined you than from an article, including this one.

## What "permanent" means on the page

Our page uses the phrase permanent hair reduction, and it is careful to say reduction. It goes on to say that some fine hair may regrow over time, typically much lighter and sparser, and that yearly touch-ups help maintain the result.

For planning purposes, that means the calendar does not end at the last session. It thins out into a once-a-year visit, like a dental cleaning. The day you finish the course, put next year's touch-up on the calendar. That is the whole maintenance plan, and it is easier to keep when it already has a date.

## A one-page plan

If you want the short version to keep on your phone, here it is.

- Pick the area or areas. Our page groups them from the face and underarms to the legs and back.
- Count the months: six to eight sessions, four to six weeks apart. Start six to ten months before the date you care about.
- Look at how much sun that window holds for the area you are treating, and tell the office about trips when you book.
- Plan the switch from waxing to shaving on the timeline your provider gives you.
- Book the consultation at whichever office is already on your way somewhere. The details, including the FAQ I quoted above, are on the [laser hair removal](https://hitchcoxaesthetics.com/laser-hair-removal) page at Sarah Hitchcox Aesthetics.
- The day you finish, put the yearly touch-up on next year's calendar.

That is it. The appointment is the easy part. The calendar is the treatment.

# Plan Wellness Appointments Around a Busy Family Calendar

*A reusable calendar method for parents fitting skin, injectable and weight-management visits around travel, childcare and follow-ups.*

By Sarah Hitchcox, RN

![An open blank weekly planner with a pen, keys and a coffee mug on a kitchen counter in morning light](images/image-1.png)
*One calendar, one color for your own appointments, and the same three lines on every entry.*

The hard part of a wellness appointment, for most parents, is not the appointment. It is everything around it. Who has the kids for that hour? Does it land the week before a trip? And what about the follow-up visit that nobody wrote down at the time?

A single appointment can be squeezed in. A series of them needs a system. The method below works for any practice, including ours at [Sarah Hitchcox Aesthetics](https://hitchcoxaesthetics.com), whether the visit is a laser session, an injectable touch-up, or a weight-management check-in. It also works for the dentist and the pediatrician.

## Start with the calendar you already use

Do not start a new calendar. Whatever your family already runs on, whether it is a shared phone calendar or the paper one on the fridge, add a category for your own health appointments and give it a color nobody else uses. If it is not on the family calendar, it is not real to the rest of the household.

Every entry gets the same three lines: the exact address, who is covering the kids, and what follow-up the visit creates. The address matters more than it sounds. Plenty of practices have more than one office. Ours has one in Bearden on Kingston Pike and one in Farragut on Campbell Station Road, and both addresses include a suite number. Put the suite in the entry. It saves a parking-lot search with a toddler in the back seat.

## Block travel and big family dates first

Before you book anything, mark the immovable things: school breaks, the beach week, tournaments, recitals, house guests, and the weekend the grandparents visit. Do this for the whole season, not just the month.

Many treatments involve a follow-up or a series of visits, and their timing is set by the treatment, not by your convenience. Different treatments are timed differently, so do not assume there is a standard window that fits before or after a trip. Ask the office directly: "I am traveling on these dates. When would you schedule this?" A good office will look at your dates and tell you.

## Decide the childcare plan before you pick the time

Parents usually have three choices: book during school or preschool hours, trade coverage with a partner or another parent, or bring the child along. Only the first two are reliable. Not every office can have a child in the treatment room, so before you assume you can bring one, ask about the policy and whether there is a waiting area.

Length varies by visit. As one example, our own site lists one injectable appointment at 10 to 15 minutes, which can fit inside a preschool drop-off window. A consultation, a laser session, or a weight-management visit runs on its own clock. When you book, ask how long to plan for, including any time before or after the treatment itself, and put that full block on the calendar rather than just the start time.

## Write the follow-up in before you leave the office

![An empty, bright treatment room with a cream reclining chair and a brass tray stand](images/image-2.png)
*Ask how long to plan for, including time before and after the treatment, and block the whole window.*

This is the step that gets missed. Some visits are one-and-done. Others are the first of several, or the start of an ongoing program with regular check-ins. [Knoxville Weight Loss Clinic](https://weightlossknoxvilletn.com), for instance, describes its physician-supervised program as a consultation, then a personalized plan, then ongoing check-ins to review progress. A program like that is a standing item on your calendar, not a single event.

So make it a rule: you do not leave with "we will call you." Before you walk out, book the next visit or at least write its expected date into your calendar as tentative. If a treatment is booked as a series, ask how many visits and how far apart, then enter every one of them, even if the later dates are placeholders. It is far easier to move a tentative appointment than to remember one that was never written down.

## A reusable template you can copy

Keep the entry short enough that you will actually fill it in. Four lines is enough:

- **Where:** office name, street, and suite number.
- **Who:** the person covering the kids, or the school hours that make coverage unnecessary.
- **Before:** anything the office asked you to do or avoid ahead of the visit, written exactly as they said it, not from memory.
- **Next:** the follow-up date, or the word "ask" if you do not know yet.

Keep the template in a note on your phone and paste it into every new appointment. The "Before" line is the one people skip, and it is the one that most often leads to a wasted trip.

## Questions worth asking when you book

A few questions, asked once, save several phone calls later. Which office will the appointment be at, and will your provider be there that day? Call the office you actually plan to visit; [Botox Knox Med Spa](https://botoxknoxvilletn.com), for example, lists separate phone numbers for its Bearden and Farragut locations. How much notice does the office need if you have to reschedule? Does this visit create a follow-up, and roughly when? And if you have travel coming up, how would they time the visit around it?

None of these are awkward. Offices answer them all day. The parent who asks at booking is the one who does not end up canceling from the carpool line.

## Do a weekly pass on the calendar

None of this holds up without a regular check. My Four and More's piece on [how big families keep a house organized](https://myfourandmore.com/how-big-families-can-keep-a-house-organized/) makes the case for a Sunday reset: one fixed time each week when the paper pile and the things leaving the house get dealt with. Your appointment calendar deserves the same five minutes.

Look at the next two weeks. Confirm childcare for anything in your color. Read the "Before" line on each entry. Check that every "Next" has a date or a reminder to ask for one. Then close the calendar and get on with the week.

The goal is not a perfect schedule. It is a calendar you trust, so that taking care of yourself stops being the first thing to fall off the list when the family calendar fills up.

# What to ask a medical weight-loss clinic before enrolling

*A nurse's checklist for comparing supervision, follow-up visits, total cost, and what a program really includes, so you can record each clinic's answers and decide with a clear head.*

By Sarah Hitchcox, RN

![An empty, bright consultation room with a cream treatment chair, a brass tray stand, and a blank notebook on a side table.](images/image-1.png)
*Bring the same list of questions to every clinic and write the answers down before you decide.*

Most people choose a weight-loss program in a single visit. They hear a friendly explanation, see a monthly figure, and sign. A few months in, they find out what was not included. I would rather you compare two or three clinics on paper first. This is a checklist for that comparison, and a way to record each clinic's answers so you decide from notes rather than from memory.

Bring the same questions to every clinic. Write the answers in the clinic's own words. If an answer is vague, write "vague" and move on. A vague answer is information too.

## Who is actually supervising you?

"Medically supervised" appears on nearly every program page. Ask what it means at this clinic. Who reviews your medical history before the first dose? Who decides on dose changes? Is that person a physician, a nurse practitioner, a registered nurse, or someone else, and will you meet them?

Some clinics state this plainly. [Knoxville Weight Loss Clinic](https://weightlossknoxvilletn.com) says on its site that its plans are managed by board-certified physicians and that the first visit reviews your health history and runs labs. That is the level of detail to look for. Whatever a clinic tells you, write down the title of the person who will be responsible for your plan.

## What happens at a follow-up visit?

A program is mostly follow-ups. The first consultation is one visit; the check-ins are the next several months. So ask how often follow-ups are scheduled, whether they are in person, by phone, or by message, and what is checked at each one. Ask who adjusts the dose and what they base the adjustment on.

Then ask what happens between visits. If you have a question about a side effect on a Saturday, who do you contact, and how quickly do they answer? Record the answer exactly. "You can always reach us" and "call the office and a nurse returns calls the same day" are different promises.

At our practice, the GLP-1 program begins with a consultation that reviews your medical history and goals, and it includes regular check-ins, dose adjustments, and lifestyle coaching. You can read how we describe it at [Sarah Hitchcox Aesthetics](https://hitchcoxaesthetics.com/weight-loss). Ask any clinic you visit, including ours, to walk you through what a typical check-in looks like.

## What is the total cost, not the monthly figure?

I am not going to quote prices here, because they change and because the headline monthly number is rarely the whole cost. Ask for the total instead: the consultation, any labs, the medication, the injection supplies, the follow-up visits, and any membership or program fee. Ask which of those recur and which are one-time. Ask what happens to the cost when your dose goes up.

![A blank open notebook and pen on a white clinic counter, with a treatment chair softly out of focus behind.](images/image-2.png)
*One sheet per clinic, the same questions in the same order, filled in during or right after the visit.*

Then ask about leaving. Is there a minimum commitment? If you stop after two months, what do you owe? Can you pause?

Ask for all of this in writing. A clinic that publishes clear pricing up front has made this easy to check. Any clinic should be willing to put its numbers in an email before you enroll.

## What is included, and what is an add-on?

Two programs can quote the same monthly figure and include very different things. Build a list with the clinic: medication, injection supplies, follow-up visits, labs, nutrition or lifestyle coaching, and messaging access. Beside each item, write "included," "extra," or "not offered."

Ask about the medication itself. What exactly is being prescribed, and where does it come from? Some clinics state that they prescribe FDA-approved medication sourced from licensed U.S. pharmacies. Ask every clinic to tell you the same about theirs, and write down the answer.

## What does realistic look like here?

Be cautious with any clinic that leads with a number. Ask instead how the clinic defines progress, how it decides whether the medication is working for you, and what it does if it is not. Ask what side effects they see and how they handle them. Ask what the plan is for the end of the program: how they decide when to change or stop the medication, and what support continues after you reach your goal.

A good answer to these questions is specific and a little unexciting. A poor answer is enthusiastic and short.

## Record the answers, then decide at home

Use one sheet per clinic, with the same questions in the same order: supervision, follow-ups, total cost, what is included, and what realistic means. Fill it in during or right after the visit. Then set the sheets side by side and give yourself a day before you enroll anywhere.

I spent years in an emergency department before I moved into this work, and one habit carried over: the useful answer is the specific one. Choose the clinic whose answers you could write down without guessing. If you could not, you have not been told enough to enroll yet, and that is worth knowing before you pay.

# Four med spa red flags a nurse would walk away from

*A Knoxville nurse injector on the warning signs you can see before anyone touches your face, and why each one matters more than the price list.*

By Sarah Hitchcox, RN

![An empty, brightly lit med spa treatment room with a white reclining chair and a brass rolling tray](images/image-1.png)
*Most of the warning signs are visible before you are ever in the chair.*

I am a registered nurse, and I own a small aesthetics practice in Knoxville. Before that I worked mostly in the emergency department, which is where I learned to notice small things before they turn into big ones. Choosing a med spa uses the same skill. Most of the warning signs are visible before you are ever in the chair. Here are the four I would not talk myself past.

For each one I will separate what you can actually see from what I think it means. The first part is fact. The second is my judgment, and you are free to weigh it differently.

## 1. No consultation, or a consultation that is really a sales pitch

What you notice: you call to ask about Botox or filler and the answer is a time slot for the injection itself. Nobody asks what you want, what you have had done before, or what medications you take. Or there is a "consultation," but it lasts three minutes and ends with a package.

Why I think it matters: the consultation is where the medical part happens. It is when someone looks at how your face moves, asks about your history, and decides whether the treatment you came in for is the right one at all. When that step is skipped, the practice is telling you it does not plan to think very hard about you.

At [Sarah Hitchcox Aesthetics](https://hitchcoxaesthetics.com), consultations are free at both our Bearden and Farragut offices, and they happen before treatment, not during it. I would rather spend fifteen minutes talking someone out of a treatment than do one that does not fit.

## 2. You cannot find out who is medically responsible

What you notice: the website lists treatments but no people. The staff wear scrubs, but nobody says what license they hold. When you ask who the medical director or supervising physician is, the answer is vague, or a name with nothing behind it.

Why I think it matters: neurotoxins, fillers, lasers and prescription weight-loss medication are medical treatments. Somewhere in that building, a specific licensed person is supposed to be answerable for them. If nobody can tell you who that is, either the arrangement is thin or the staff have never been asked. Neither is reassuring.

A practice with its house in order tends to say so plainly. Look at how [Knoxville Weight Loss Clinic](https://weightlossknoxvilletn.com) puts it: every plan is managed by board-certified physicians, and the consultation reviews your health history and runs labs before anyone decides whether semaglutide or tirzepatide is right for you. You do not have to dig for it. That is what "supervised" should look like on a page.

## 3. Pressure to buy today

![A blank intake clipboard, a pen and a hand mirror on a white consultation desk](images/image-2.png)
*The consultation is where the medical part happens.*

What you notice: a discount that expires when you leave the room. A package of six sessions offered before you have had one. A suggestion that you "add" an area you did not ask about, made while you are already lying back.

Why I think it matters: urgency is a sales tool, and it works because it stops you thinking. In a clinical setting that is backwards. A good injector wants you to go home, sleep on it, and come back sure. Specials exist, and I run them, but a special should be something you can take a week to decide on. If the price goes up the moment you hesitate, the practice is built around the sale, not the result.

The clearest test is whether you can leave a consultation having bought nothing and still feel welcome to come back. If that feels awkward, notice it.

## 4. Credentials you cannot check

What you notice: titles like "master injector" or "aesthetic specialist" that are not licenses. Certificates on the wall from weekend courses, with no nursing, nurse practitioner, physician assistant or medical license alongside them. A provider who bristles when you ask.

Why I think it matters: "injector" is not a license. In my case the credential is RN, and you can look it up on the state nursing board's website in about a minute. Weekend training is real and it matters, but it sits on top of a license, not in place of one. [Botox Knox Med Spa](https://botoxknoxvilletn.com) in West Knoxville puts "board-certified providers" and "FDA-approved products" on the front of its site, and that is the right instinct. Those are the two things you should be able to check before you walk in: who is treating you, and what is going in.

Asking is not rude. Anyone who has earned a credential is usually glad to talk about it.

## What is not a red flag

A small practice is not a red flag. A nurse rather than a doctor holding the syringe is not one either, as long as the supervision behind that nurse is real and has a name. A clinic that is quiet on a Tuesday afternoon is not one.

What I would weigh instead is how easily the answers come. When a practice is doing things properly, the consultation, the supervising physician, the license and the freedom to say no are all boring facts they will tell you without being pushed. They may even seem a little surprised you asked.

If any of the four signs above show up, you do not need to argue about it or explain yourself. You just book somewhere else.

# Four Questions I Ask at Every Early GLP-1 Check-In

*The first weeks on semaglutide or tirzepatide are mostly about the stomach, the water bottle, and the plate. Here is what a nurse listens for at follow-up, and when a phone call beats waiting.*

By Sarah Hitchcox, RN

![An empty, calm clinic consultation room with a cream treatment chair and a gold tray stand holding a glass of water.](images/image-1.png)
*The early check-in is mostly listening: how the stomach felt, what was in the bottle, what was on the plate.*

Most people who start a GLP-1 medication for weight loss expect the appetite change. What surprises them is everything around it: the queasy mornings, the odd fullness after four bites, the afternoon when they realize they have not had a glass of water since breakfast.

I am a registered nurse. I spent most of my career in the emergency department before I began practicing aesthetics and medically supervised weight loss at [Sarah Hitchcox Aesthetics](https://hitchcoxaesthetics.com) in Knoxville, and I still think like a triage nurse. The early weeks on a GLP-1 are not a time to tough things out quietly. They are a time to notice, write down, and report. Here are the four questions I ask at every early check-in, and why each one matters.

## 1. How is your stomach, and when?

Nausea is the side effect people hear about most. For many it shows up in the first days after a dose and eases as the week goes on. That pattern matters. I want to know not just whether you felt sick but when, how long it lasted, and whether it was worse after a particular meal.

Timing tells us something. Queasiness after a large or greasy dinner is different from queasiness after every meal. Fullness that lasts a few hours is different from a stomach that never seems to empty. One is often something we can manage with how you eat. The other is something the prescribing physician needs to hear about before the next dose adjustment.

Keep a simple note on your phone: the date, whether it was a dose day, what you ate, how you felt. It takes thirty seconds, and it makes your check-in far more useful than "I felt kind of off."

## 2. What did you drink today?

This is the question people most often answer with a pause. When appetite drops, thirst tends to drop with it. Many patients tell me they simply forgot to drink because nothing prompted them to.

Low fluid intake makes almost every other early complaint harder to sort out. Headaches, tiredness, lightheadedness when standing, and constipation all get muddier when someone is running dry. So I ask about water before I ask about anything else on the list.

The practical fix is unglamorous: a bottle you can see, filled in the morning, finished by dinner. If plain water is hard to get down while you feel queasy, say so. That is exactly the kind of small problem a check-in is for.

## 3. What is actually on the plate?

![A full water bottle, a small plate of eggs and berries, and a phone face down on a sunny kitchen counter.](images/image-2.png)
*A bottle you can see and a small protein-forward meal solve more early GLP-1 complaints than people expect.*

Eating less is the point. Eating badly is not. When someone is only hungry for a few bites, what those bites are made of matters more than it used to.

At early check-ins I ask people to walk me through a real day, not the ideal one. Often the pattern is coffee, a skipped lunch, and a small dinner that is mostly bread or pasta. That leaves people feeling weak and irritable, and it is not the way anyone wants to lose weight.

The nutrition guidance that comes with a supervised program is built for exactly this. At [Knoxville Weight Loss Clinic](https://weightlossknoxvilletn.com), the plan is not just the medication and a dosage schedule. It includes nutrition coaching and regular check-ins where the physician monitors progress and adjusts the dose. Protein comes up at nearly every one of those visits, because it is the part of the plate that quietly disappears when appetite falls. We would rather see you eat a small, protein-forward meal than skip and then feel unwell.

## 4. What made you wonder whether to call?

This is my favorite question, because the answer is almost always something the person talked themselves out of mentioning.

Here is my rule from years of triage: if you found yourself wondering whether a symptom was worth a call, it was worth a call. That is not the same as saying every symptom is an emergency. It means the clinic would rather hear about a small thing early than a big thing late.

Call sooner rather than later if you cannot keep fluids down, if nausea or vomiting is not letting up, if you have belly pain that is more than ordinary discomfort, or if you feel faint. Those are the things the prescribing physician wants to know about between visits, not at the next scheduled one. A supervised program has patient support for a reason. Use it.

And do not stop or change your dose on your own because one week was rough. Say so at the check-in, or before it. Dose adjustment is a decision the physician makes with the full picture, and the full picture includes how you felt.

## Why the check-in is the safety net

Everything above works because someone is actually asking. The consultation at the start reviews your health history and runs labs. The check-ins afterward are where side effects get caught, where the dose gets tuned, and where the eating pattern gets corrected before it costs you strength.

One more note for anyone seen at our Bearden or Farragut offices. If you have a Botox or Dysport visit booked with our injectors at [Botox Knox Med Spa](https://botoxknoxvilletn.com) while you are in the early weeks of a GLP-1, mention the medication to whoever is treating you. It is one more piece of the picture, and we like the whole picture.

The first weeks on a GLP-1 are usually manageable. They go better when you keep a note, keep a bottle filled, keep protein on the plate, and keep the clinic's number where you can find it.

# How to Read Med Spa Reviews Like a Nurse

*A five-star average tells you the mood of a waiting room. It does not tell you who held the syringe. Here is what I look for in a review, and what I skip.*

By Sarah Hitchcox, RN

![An empty white treatment chair beside a brass tray stand in a bright clinic room](images/image-1.png)
*A review can describe a room like this one. It cannot tell you who will be standing in it.*

I am a registered nurse who owns a small aesthetics practice in Knoxville, Tennessee. Before that I worked in the emergency department. Both jobs taught me the same habit: separate what someone observed from what they concluded about it. Most parents I meet have read a page of reviews before they ever call. Here is how I read that page, including the reviews on my own website.

## What does a star rating actually measure?

A star average measures how people felt when they left. That is real information, but it is a mood, not a chart note. A rating cannot tell you who did the injection, what training that person had, or what was done when something did not go to plan.

My own homepage shows a rating and a count, with three short quotes underneath. I know exactly what it leaves out, which is why I would rather you read the reviews than count the stars.

## What does a useful review say?

A useful review sounds like a report. It names things that could be checked.

Who did the work: "Sarah did my appointment" is more useful than "the staff was amazing." At [Sarah Hitchcox Aesthetics](https://hitchcoxaesthetics.com), every treatment is performed by me, and I want a review to say so. A reader should know whether the person being praised is the person they will actually see.

What the visit was for: One of the reviews on my site mentions an appointment for jaw clenching. That single detail says the clinic treats that concern, and that the patient knew what she came in for.

What was explained: Reviews that mention the provider explaining what would work for their skin, or taking the time to answer every question, are describing a consultation. That is the part of the visit that protects you. A place that explains is usually a place that will also tell you no.

What happened over time: "I have been seeing her for about a year" is a different statement from "just left, loved it." The first person has had follow-up visits. Look for reviewers who came back.

## What does marketing sound like?

![A phone lying face down next to a coffee mug and a notepad on a kitchen table](images/image-2.png)
*Most parents read the reviews before they ever call. Reading them well takes only a few minutes more.*

Marketing is not lying. It is written to be repeated, not to be checked. You can recognize it by a few habits.

Superlatives with no object: "Best in the state" cannot be verified by the person who wrote it, let alone by you.

Results as a promise: A review that says you will look ten years younger is describing one face and predicting yours. Faces do not work that way, and a careful provider will not let a website suggest they do.

Reviews that read like the homepage: When ten reviews in a row use the same phrasing as the clinic's own copy, someone was coached. Real people write in their own words, with details nobody would have thought to suggest.

No person named: Testimonials that only praise "the team" leave you no way to find out whether the person who earned the praise still works there.

## What can a review not tell you?

It cannot tell you whether a treatment is right for you. That depends on your health history, your medications, and whether you are pregnant or breastfeeding, none of which a stranger's five stars can weigh. That is a consultation question. We hold consultations at both of our offices, in Bearden and Farragut, and the point of them is to work out whether something should be done at all, not only how.

A review also cannot tell you how a practice is set up. [Botox Knox Med Spa](https://botoxknoxvilletn.com) in West Knoxville lists board-certified providers and sees people who drive in from Farragut, Maryville, Oak Ridge and Hardin Valley. That is useful to know, and no reviewer would think to mention it. The [Knoxville Weight Loss Clinic](https://weightlossknoxvilletn.com) runs on a physician-supervised model, with labs at the first visit and regular check-ins afterward. A review that says "great experience" will not tell you whether those check-ins happened. Ask.

## How do I read them, in practice?

Sort by most recent, not by highest rating. Read the three-star reviews first, because they are usually written by people trying to be fair. Then read the one-star reviews and, more importantly, the replies. A calm, specific reply from the owner shows you how the practice handles a problem, which matters more than how it handles a compliment. Finally, look for one review that describes the visit you are thinking of booking. If you cannot find one, that is a fair thing to bring up when you call.

If you have a review you cannot decide how to read, I am happy to think it through with you in the comments. I would also like to know which details you have found most useful, and which you have learned to skip.

Sarah Hitchcox, RN, is a Knoxville native and registered nurse with a background in emergency medicine. She owns an aesthetics practice with offices in Bearden and Farragut, Tennessee, and is currently working toward her Doctor of Nursing Practice degree.

# Why Weight Management and Facial Aesthetics Deserve Separate Plans

*They often come up in the same conversation, but a medical weight program and a facial treatment answer different questions, and keeping them apart makes both easier to judge.*

By Sarah Hitchcox, RN

![An empty, bright medical aesthetics treatment room with a white chair, a gold tray stand, and a notebook and hand mirror on a side counter.](images/image-1.png)
*A weight program and a facial treatment are measured differently, so it helps to think of them as two separate plans.*

If you have looked into healthy aging lately, you have probably noticed that two very different subjects keep landing in the same conversation. One is weight management, which has moved into ordinary medical care as prescription GLP-1 medications have become common. The other is facial aesthetics, meaning treatments aimed at lines, volume, and skin texture. People ask about both in the same breath, and that is understandable.

The trouble starts when the two are treated as one project. They are not. As a nurse who works in aesthetics, I think the most useful thing I can do here is lay out what each one actually involves, where the overlap is real, and where it is mostly marketing.

## Two Goals That Get Mentioned Together

Weight management is a medical goal. It is measured on a scale, in lab results, and in how you feel over months. Facial aesthetics is a cosmetic goal. It is about a specific feature, such as the lines between your brows or the fullness of your lips, and whether you want it to look different.

Those are different questions with different answers, handled by different kinds of providers. A good sign is when a clinic is clear about which one it is addressing, and a poor sign is when one conversation promises to fix both at once.

## What Medical Weight Management Actually Involves

A medical weight program is built around a prescription and supervision. At a physician-supervised clinic such as [Knoxville Weight Loss Clinic](https://weightlossknoxvilletn.com), the process described on its site starts with a medical evaluation that reviews your health history and runs labs to decide whether semaglutide or tirzepatide is appropriate for you. From there, the physician sets a plan with the medication, a dosage schedule, and nutrition guidance, and follow-up visits are used to check progress and adjust the dose.

Notice what is not in that description. There is no mention of your face. Weight medication is prescribed for weight and the health conditions that travel with it. It is not an aesthetic treatment, and a clinic that frames it as one is describing something the medicine was not built to do.

## What Facial Aesthetic Treatments Actually Address

Facial treatments are the opposite in scale. Each one is aimed at a defined feature. Botox, for example, temporarily blocks the nerve signals to specific facial muscles so they contract less deeply, which softens the lines those muscles make. The areas most often treated are forehead lines, crow's feet, and the vertical lines between the brows. Dermal fillers are used for volume and contour in areas such as the cheeks and lips.

![Overhead view of a scale and tape measure on one side, a hand mirror and skincare bottle on the other, with a blank two-column notebook between them.](images/image-2.png)
*Writing each goal down with the thing it is measured by keeps a medical question and a cosmetic question from blurring together.*

At [Sarah Hitchcox Aesthetics](https://hitchcoxaesthetics.com), the services fall into injectables, laser treatments, microneedling, and medical grade skincare, with radiofrequency skin tightening offered for the jawline, cheeks, and neck. Every one of those is a local treatment for a local concern. None of them changes what the scale says, and none is meant to.

## Where the Two Get Confused

The confusion usually lives in the neck and jaw. Kybella is an injectable that destroys fat cells under the chin. Masseter Botox relaxes the muscle at the angle of the jaw, which is why it is offered for jaw slimming and is also used for TMJ. Both are listed among the injectable services at [Botox Knox Med Spa](https://botoxknoxvilletn.com), and both change the shape of the lower face.

Neither is weight loss. A treatment that reduces a pocket of fat under the chin or relaxes a jaw muscle is working on a few square inches. It does not touch body weight, metabolism, or the health markers a weight program is monitoring. If anyone suggests an injectable as a route to losing weight, that is a mismatch between the tool and the goal.

## The Weight Loss and Skin Question, Honestly

The question I hear most often is whether losing weight will change your face. I want to be careful here, because this is where the evidence available to me runs thin. The clinic pages I have drawn on for this article do not make any claim about how weight change affects facial skin or volume, and I am not going to invent one to fill the gap.

What I can say is narrower. How a face looks after a change in weight varies from person to person, and it depends on factors that can only be assessed by someone examining you in person. An article cannot tell you what your own face will do. A provider who has seen it can at least tell you what they observe and what, if anything, they would suggest, and they should be willing to say when the honest answer is that they do not know yet.

## How to Keep Your Own Goals Straight

A simple habit helps. When you are thinking about either of these, write the goal in one sentence and name what it is measured by. "I want to lose weight and improve my lab numbers" is a medical goal, and it belongs with a physician-supervised program. "I want the lines between my brows to be less deep" is an aesthetic goal, and it belongs with an injector.

If you find yourself writing one sentence that contains both, split it. Then ask each provider only the question that is theirs to answer. Whether the two plans should happen at the same time, in a particular order, or not at all is a decision for the clinicians who actually see you, not for a general article.

Healthy aging is a long project, and it is easier to manage when each part of it has a clear owner. Keep the weight conversation medical and the facial conversation specific, and you will find both are easier to evaluate and easier to walk away from when something does not add up.

# Making Room for Your Own Kind of Self-Care in a Wedding Year

*A plain guide to keeping some ordinary time for yourself in the twelve months before a wedding, without letting the planning take all of it.*

By Sarah Hitchcox, RN

![Editorial illustration of a bright white treatment room with a white reclining chair and a slim gold rolling tray holding a closed linen planner and a small bunch of white ranunculus with eucalyptus](images/image-1.png)
*Editorial illustration inspired by the practice’s treatment room, with a planner and flowers.*

Wedding planning fills every free evening. Between the venue, the vendors and the fittings, the months before a wedding can turn into one long to-do list, and the things you normally do for yourself are the first to fall off it. The morning walk goes. The standing nail appointment goes. The one evening a week with nothing in it goes.

This is a guide to keeping some of that. None of it is required. You do not need to change anything about how you look to have a good wedding, and you will look like yourself in the photos either way. The point is to protect a little ordinary time during a year that will try to claim all of it.

## Start with what is already fixed

Write the wedding date at the top of a page. Under it, list every commitment that already has a date: engagement photos, dress fittings, the shower, the rehearsal dinner, family travel, the work deadline that lands the same month, the friend's wedding you are also attending.

Put them all on one page or in one calendar view. Seeing them together does most of the work. You can spot the crowded stretches, the weeks where three things stack up, and the quieter weeks where there is still some air.

## Leave some time deliberately empty

Once the fixed items are down, resist the urge to fill every gap. Block off a few evenings a month, or one weekend morning, that stay blank on purpose.

Unscheduled time is what absorbs the surprises: the vendor who cancels, the family conversation that runs long, the week you are simply tired. It is also where rest lives. Treat a blank block as an appointment with yourself that you are allowed to keep.

## Reserve room for routines you have chosen

Self-care in a wedding year does not need to be new or elaborate. Often the most useful thing is to keep doing what already works for you: the walk, the skin-care routine you already have, enough sleep, water, and the hair or nail appointment you have kept for years. If a home manicure is part of your routine, StyleMotivation's guide to [habits for a longer-lasting home manicure](https://www.stylemotivation.com/5-good-habits-to-adopt-long-lasting-home-manicure/) is a practical place to start.

Decide which of these matter to you, and give each one a standing slot on the calendar so it is not renegotiated every week.

## If you are considering a clinical service, ask a clinician about timing

Some people also think about professional services during a wedding year: a skin treatment, an injectable, a laser series. Whether to do any of that is entirely personal, and deciding not to is just as good an answer as deciding to.

If you are considering one, the right move is not to find a schedule in an article. Ask the provider directly, with your calendar in hand: what does the whole process involve, how would it fit around your specific dates, and what is realistic for you. [Sarah Hitchcox Aesthetics](https://hitchcoxaesthetics.com) is a registered-nurse-led practice with offices in Bearden and Farragut that offers consultations to discuss goals and build a personalized plan. That conversation is where individualized scheduling belongs.

It also helps to read how a provider describes its own approach before you book anything. [Botox Knox Med Spa](https://botoxknoxvilletn.com) in West Knoxville, for instance, lists a natural-results focus on its site. A stated approach like that helps you decide whether you even want the conversation.

## Weight is health care, not wedding preparation

A wedding year comes with a lot of pressure to change your body for one day. It is worth saying plainly that you do not have to. Weight is a health matter, and health decisions belong on their own timeline, with a physician, for reasons that have nothing to do with a dress.

If someone is already working with a clinician on weight management, that continues at the pace the clinician sets. [Knoxville Weight Loss Clinic](https://weightlossknoxvilletn.com), for example, describes its program as physician-supervised, beginning with a consultation that reviews health history and labs and continuing with regular check-ins. That is the shape of ongoing medical care. A wedding date is not a reason to start it, rush it, or change it.

## The one-page version for the fridge

- Every fixed commitment on one page, so you can see the crowded weeks.
- A few blank blocks each month that stay blank.
- A standing slot for each routine you already like.
- Any question about a clinical service goes to a clinician, with your dates in hand.
- Weight decisions stay with your physician, on your own timeline.

If you do none of this, you will still have a wedding, and you will still look like yourself, which is the whole point. If you do some of it, you get through the year with a little of your own time intact.

# Keeping Your Own Beauty Goals When Social Media Changes Its Mind

*A nurse's case for deciding what you like about your face before the feed decides for you.*

By Sarah Hitchcox, RN

![A hand mirror, a closed notebook and a pencil on a pale wooden dressing table in soft window light](images/image-1.png)
*Decide what you like about your face before the feed decides for you.*

Every few months the feed changes its mind. Thin brows come back, then thick brows. Full lips are in, then "overdone" lips are out and everyone is talking about dissolving them. A filter that makes skin look like glass is everywhere, and then it is embarrassing. If you follow beauty content at all, you have watched this cycle more than once.

I am a registered nurse working in aesthetics in Knoxville, Tennessee, with a background primarily in the emergency department. What follows is not a treatment and not a rule. It is a way of looking at your own face before the feed looks at it for you.

## A trend is a group decision. Your face is not.

Trends are not wrong, exactly. They are just made by a lot of people at once, for reasons that have nothing to do with you. A look spreads because it photographs well under a ring light, or because one person with a large following tried it in a good week. Then it becomes the standard for a while, and then it does not.

Your face was not in the meeting. It has its own proportions, its own way of moving when you laugh, and its own history. Some of what you see in the mirror you would happily change. Some of it you would miss if it were gone. Only you know which is which, and that knowledge is worth more than any trend cycle.

## Write down what you already like

Here is a plain exercise. Before you look at anyone else's face, look at your own and name three things you like about it. Not things you tolerate. Things you would defend.

Then name the one or two things that bother you when nobody is around to tell you they should. Those are the honest goals. They tend to be small and specific: the line between the brows that reads as anger when you are not angry, or the tired look that lasts after the tiredness is over.

Everything else on the list, the things that only bother you after twenty minutes of scrolling, can wait. Most of them will wait forever, and you will not miss them.

## Leaving it alone is a valid choice

Somewhere along the way, doing nothing started to look like falling behind. It is not. Leaving a feature alone is a decision, and it is often the right one.

Even the way a treatment is described can help you decide what you actually want. The [Botox](https://hitchcoxaesthetics.com/botox) page at Sarah Hitchcox Aesthetics, for example, describes the aim as relaxing the muscles that cause wrinkles while preserving your natural expressions. Read that way, the thing worth protecting is the expression. A face that still moves like yours is the whole point, and no trend gets a vote on that.

The same applies to any decision about your appearance, with or without a clinic involved. If you cannot say in your own words why you want a change, the want probably is not yours yet. That is fine. Let it sit.

## Choose your sources carefully

If you do want outside input, choose it carefully. Useful sources say what something does and what it does not do, talk about proportion rather than transformation, and are comfortable telling you a look would not suit you.

It also helps to read how a provider describes its own approach before you ever book anything. The West Knoxville injectables practice [Botox Knox Med Spa](https://botoxknoxvilletn.com), for instance, lists a natural-results focus on its site. A stated approach like that is something you can hold a provider to, and it is a calmer thing to keep in your feed than the trend cycle, because it will still say the same thing next year.

## What stays when the feed moves on

The trend will change again before this post is old. What will not change is the list you made: the things you like, the one or two things that genuinely bother you, and the decision to leave the rest alone.

Keep that list somewhere you can find it. Read it before you read the comments. The feed is allowed to change its mind. You are allowed not to.

*The first follow-up on a GLP-1 is less about the scale than about tolerance: nausea, fluids, and what a day of eating has become.*

Most of what people read about GLP-1 medications is about the end of the story: the weight that comes off over a year or more. This article is about the beginning. The first few weeks on semaglutide or tirzepatide are when side effects are most likely, when the dose is still being adjusted, and when a scheduled follow-up does the most good.

I am a registered nurse with a background in emergency care, so with any new medication I want to know what is common, what should pass, and what is the signal to call. Nothing here replaces your own prescriber's instructions. It is meant to explain why they exist.

## Why the dose starts low

Both medications begin low and rise in steps. The Wegovy (semaglutide) label starts adults at 0.25 mg once a week for four weeks, then steps up about every four weeks toward a maintenance dose [1]. The Zepbound (tirzepatide) label starts at 2.5 mg once a week and increases in 2.5 mg steps, each held for at least four weeks [2].

The stepped schedule is the main tool for keeping side effects tolerable. Each increase can bring a few rough days, and the labels let prescribers slow down: Wegovy's says to consider delaying the next increase by four weeks if a dose is not tolerated, and Zepbound's says to consider a lower maintenance dose [1, 2]. The follow-up visit is where that decision gets made.

## What the trials recorded

Nausea is the most common side effect, and the real numbers help. In the adult trials summarized in the Wegovy label, nausea was reported by 44 percent of people on the 2.4 mg dose, diarrhea by 30 percent, and vomiting and constipation by 24 percent each [1]. In the Zepbound trials at the 15 mg dose, nausea was reported by 28 percent versus 8 percent on placebo, and diarrhea by 23 percent [2].

In the 68-week STEP 1 trial of semaglutide, nausea and diarrhea were typically transient, mild to moderate, and subsided with time, yet 4.5 percent of participants stopped the drug because of gastrointestinal events, against 0.8 percent on placebo [3]. In the SURMOUNT-1 trial of tirzepatide, gastrointestinal events were also mostly mild to moderate and occurred primarily during dose escalation [4].

Put plainly: stomach symptoms are common, most people get through them, and they cluster around the weeks when the dose is changing, which is exactly when follow-ups are scheduled.

## Nausea and the size of the plate

These medications slow how quickly the stomach empties. That is part of how they reduce appetite, and it is the likely reason a normal-sized meal can suddenly feel like too much.

A 2024 review in the journal Obesity, written for clinicians, recommends checking protein, fiber, micronutrient, and fluid intake before treatment and monitoring during it, so that stomach symptoms or inadequate intake are caught early [5]. The first follow-up questions are simple. How big are your meals? How fast do you eat? What happens after a rich meal compared with a plain one? A short note on your phone, with the date, the dose, and how you felt, answers those far better than memory.

## Fluids: the side effect that hides behind the appetite

When appetite drops, thirst often drops with it, and someone who is also vomiting or having diarrhea can lose fluid faster than they replace it. Both labels warn specifically about acute kidney injury from volume depletion and tell prescribers to watch kidney function in patients reporting severe stomach symptoms, especially when starting or raising the dose [1, 2].

Nobody feels their kidneys. What a clinician can notice is a patient who is lightheaded on standing, urinating much less than usual, or unable to keep fluids down. Those belong in your notes and out loud at the visit.

## Protein and what is on the plate

Eating less is the point of the medication, but eating less of everything is not. The same review lists protein first among the intakes to check before and during treatment, alongside fiber, vitamins and minerals, and fluids [5]. On a smaller appetite the easy foods tend to win, and protein is often the first thing to slide. It helps to make protein the first thing on the plate, in smaller and more frequent portions, which also fits the way the medication changes fullness.

## What a follow-up visit is for

A follow-up in the first month or two is not mainly a weigh-in. It is a check of tolerance before the next dose step, where your prescriber decides whether to move up on schedule, hold the current dose longer, or step back. The labels make that a normal part of the plan, not a sign of failure [1, 2]. It is also where side effects get sorted: the expected and passing, the ones that call for a change in dose or eating pattern, and the rare ones that need urgent attention.

## When to call instead of waiting

Some symptoms should not wait for the next appointment. The prescribing information for both drugs tells patients to stop the medication and contact their prescriber promptly for severe, persistent abdominal pain, with or without vomiting, which can signal pancreatitis, and to report possible gallbladder symptoms such as upper abdominal pain, fever, or yellowing of the skin or eyes [1, 2].

Vomiting or diarrhea that keeps you from holding down fluids belongs in the same category, because of the kidney warning above. So does any sign of low blood sugar, such as shakiness, sweating, or confusion, in someone who also takes insulin or a sulfonylurea [1, 2]. And if you have surgery or a procedure with anesthesia coming up, tell that team you are on a GLP-1, because both labels now warn about food remaining in the stomach during anesthesia [1, 2].

None of this is a reason to avoid the medication. It is a reason to keep the follow-up schedule, keep the short notes, and know in advance which symptoms mean call today.

# Who Owns the Follow-up? A Nurse's Checklist for Digital Patient Messages

*Online booking and patient messaging move clinical work into an inbox. Before a practice adopts or keeps either, it should be able to answer four questions about ownership, escalation, acknowledgment and handoff.*

By Sarah Hitchcox, RN

![Empty clinic reception counter with a closed laptop, desk phone and notepad in a bright white office.](images/image-1.png)
*Every digital message a practice accepts needs a person's name on it, not just a queue.*

Most outpatient practices now take appointment requests and patient questions through a digital channel: a booking page, a portal inbox, a text line. These tools are sold on convenience, and they deliver it. What they do not deliver on their own is an answer to the question every nurse eventually asks about a message that went unanswered: who owned this?

Nursing has always been the profession that notices the follow-up nobody claimed. What is new is volume. One health system analysis published in the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association found that patient portal messages rose sharply during the pandemic and stayed elevated. Under the 21st Century Cures Act rules, patients also see results and notes on release, which produces more questions, sooner. A workflow that was tolerable at ten messages a day can quietly fail at forty.

The checklist below is not about choosing software. It evaluates any booking or messaging workflow, existing or proposed, by the four moments where follow-up is most often lost.

## 1. Ownership: one name, not one queue

Ask who owns each message from arrival until it is closed. The answer should be a role, and at any given hour that role should resolve to a single person. "The front desk" or "the clinical team" is a queue, not an owner.

When a message arrives after hours, whose name is on it in the morning? When the owner is off, who is the owner? Can anyone see who is responsible for an open message without asking around? If the tool cannot show that, the practice needs a written rule that does.

## 2. Escalation: what makes a message clinical

Booking requests and billing questions can wait for business hours. A message describing new swelling, trouble breathing, a medication reaction, or a symptom the patient is frightened by cannot. Someone qualified to recognize a clinical problem has to sort these.

Who reads the message first, and does that person have the training to spot an escalation trigger? Is there a written list of triggers that everyone who touches the inbox knows? What is the longest a clinical message can sit before a licensed person sees it? The Joint Commission's root cause data has for years placed communication failures among the leading contributors to sentinel events. Most of those failures are not dramatic. They are a message read by the wrong person at the wrong time.

## 3. Acknowledgment: the patient should not have to guess

Automatic confirmations solve half of this. "We received your request" tells the patient the message did not vanish. It does not say when a person will act on it, and it does not tell the practice that anyone has.

What does the patient get, and when? What does the staff see, and when? A sound workflow makes both visible: the patient knows the expected response window, and the team can see which messages have passed it. If the only acknowledgment is the automated one, the practice has acknowledged receipt but not responsibility.

## 4. Handoff: where most follow-up dies

Follow-up rarely fails in the middle of one person's shift. It fails at the seam: end of day, a message that starts as scheduling and turns clinical, a reply that needs a provider's decision first. Each is a handoff, and each needs to be recorded somewhere other than someone's memory.

When a message changes hands, where is that written? Is there a daily review of anything still open, and who runs it? Can a message be closed without a documented outcome? If the honest answer to the last question is yes, the practice will eventually close a message that should have been a phone call.

## Using the checklist

Run these questions against the workflow the practice already has, and write the answers down. Then ask the vendor of any new tool the same four questions and count how many the product answers and how many fall to policy. Most fall to policy. That is not a mark against the tool. It is the reason a nurse should be in the room when the workflow is designed.

Ownership, escalation, acknowledgment, handoff. If a practice can name who does each of those and show where it is documented, its digital front door is a clinical workflow. If it cannot, it is an inbox.
