# A Botox Decision That Is Yours, Even When Everyone Has an Opinion

*A Knoxville nurse injector on sorting your own reasons from everyone else's before you book anything.*

By Sarah Hitchcox, RN

Somebody in your life has an opinion about Botox. A friend who swears by it and wants you to come along. A mother who thinks you are too young. A comment section. By the time most people sit down in my chair for the first time, they have heard a dozen opinions and are not sure which one is theirs.

I am a registered nurse who spent most of my career in an emergency department before moving into aesthetics, and I own a practice in Knoxville. I inject Botox for a living, so I am not neutral about it. But I do not think everyone should get it, and I would rather you decide slowly than book because someone talked you into it. Here is how I would think it through.

## Start with what you actually see

Other people's opinions are about them. The only useful starting point is your own face, in a normal mirror, in normal light. Is there a line between your brows that stays when your face is relaxed? Do the horizontal lines across your forehead bother you, or did someone else point them out? Is there something you keep noticing in photos, or something you only noticed after a friend mentioned her own?

Botox treats a specific problem. It is a neuromodulator that temporarily blocks nerve signals to certain facial muscles so they cannot contract as deeply. That softens the lines those muscles make, most often the "11s" between the brows, forehead lines and crow's feet. If the thing you dislike is not made by a muscle, Botox is not the answer, however many people recommend it.

## Separate the pressure from the reasons

Write down, honestly, why this is on your mind. Then sort the list into two columns.

One column is pressure from other people: a friend wants company, a partner made a comment, everyone at work seems to be doing it, a video told you that you are behind. The other column is your own reasons: you have looked at one line for two years and would like it softer, or the women in your family etch deep frown lines and you would rather stay ahead of it.

Neither column makes you shallow. But only the second column is a reason to book. If the first column is full and the second is empty, that is your answer for now, and there is nothing wrong with "not yet."

## Questions worth asking yourself first

Before you talk to any injector, sit with these:

- What specifically do I want to look different, and what do I want left alone?
- Would I still want this if nobody I know ever found out?
- Am I hoping it changes how I feel about something else, like a breakup or a birthday?
- Do I understand that the effect is temporary, and am I fine deciding about it again later?
- Am I okay with a result that is subtle rather than dramatic?
- Can I fit this into my life without it becoming one more thing to stress about?

If you get through that list and still want to know more, the next step is a consultation, not a treatment appointment. At [Sarah Hitchcox Aesthetics](https://hitchcoxaesthetics.com/botox) that conversation is about your goals and a plan that fits your face, including whether Botox or Dysport suits your muscle strength and anatomy better. You are allowed to leave without booking anything.

## What "natural" means to me

The fear I hear most is looking frozen, or looking like someone else. That worry is reasonable, and it should shape who you choose. My approach is to relax the muscles that cause the lines while keeping your expressions. I would rather accentuate what is already yours than change it. An injector who listens when you say "I still want to raise my eyebrows" is doing the job right.

That standard should hold anywhere you go. It is the same one [Botox Knox Med Spa](https://botoxknoxvilletn.com) in West Knoxville puts on its front page: locally owned, board-certified providers, and a natural results focus.

## Deciding no is a complete decision

You do not owe anyone a reason. If you weigh it and decide Botox is not for you, that is a full answer, and it stays true until you change your mind. If you decide yes, make sure it is yes to your own reasons, in your own words, to an injector who wrote them down before picking up a syringe.

Everyone will still have an opinion. Yours is the one that counts.

# Lip Filler Goals: What to Bring to the Conversation Before Booking

*A nurse injector on how to describe what you want your lips to do, not just how you want them to look.*

By Sarah Hitchcox, RN

I inject lips for a living, and the most useful thing a new patient brings me is not a photo of someone famous. It is a clear sentence about her own mouth: what bothers her, and what she wants to keep. Here is what I would put together before you book.

## Start with your own lips, not someone else's

Reference photos are fine. Use them to point at one thing, like the way a lower lip catches light, rather than as a whole face you want to borrow. Lips sit on top of bone and muscle that are yours alone, and at [Sarah Hitchcox Aesthetics](https://hitchcoxaesthetics.com/filler) we look at bone structure and tissue quality before deciding where any volume belongs.

More useful than a celebrity photo is a photo of you. Take one relaxed and one smiling, straight on, no filter. "I like my shape and want a little more of it" and "my top lip disappears when I smile" are different problems, and they are treated differently. Bring both photos.

## Learn three words: volume, shape, definition

Lip filler can change volume, shape, and definition. Those are three separate goals. Volume is how full the lips are. Shape is the outline, including the cupid's bow and how the lower lip sits against the upper. Definition is the edge, the border between lip and skin.

Before booking, decide which one you actually mean when you say "better." Many people who ask for volume want definition. Naming it keeps you from paying for something you did not want.

## Know that "a little" has a unit

Filler comes in syringes, and our lip appointments are booked as a half syringe or a full syringe. So "just a little" is a real quantity, and it is worth asking what your injector would start with and why.

Ask what product she plans to use, too. Most modern fillers are hyaluronic acid, a substance the body already makes, and different fillers have different densities. Lips generally get a softer product than a chin or jawline. If the answer is the same product for every area, ask why.

## Ask whether you want filler at all

Some people who ask about lip filler actually want the upper lip to show more when they smile. That can be a Botox lip flip conversation instead. A lip flip is a subtle technique that creates a fuller-looking upper lip without filler, and it is one of the treatments offered at [Botox Knox Med Spa](https://botoxknoxvilletn.com). It does not add volume. It relaxes the muscle so the lip turns out slightly.

You do not need to know which one you want before booking. You need to know your goal well enough that the injector can tell you which tool fits it.

## Bring your calendar

A filler appointment typically takes under an hour, and you can see the change immediately. There may be minor swelling or bruising afterward, which subsides. Do not book two days before the photos you care about. Give yourself a buffer.

Ask how long to expect your result to last. Our filler page lists a range of six months to two years across all areas, and lips are one specific case within that range, so ask about lips directly. Ask about comfort as well. We use numbing cream and fillers that contain lidocaine.

## Ask about the exit

This is the question most people skip. Hyaluronic acid fillers can be dissolved with an enzyme called hyaluronidase if needed. If you simply stop getting filler, your lips gradually return to how they looked before as the product metabolizes. Ask whether the product is hyaluronic acid, and ask whether the practice dissolves filler itself. Those two answers tell you a lot about how much control you keep.

## What I would write down before you book

Keep it to one screen on your phone:

- The one thing about your lips that bothers you.
- The one thing you want to keep.
- Which word you mean: volume, shape, or definition.
- Your next event and the date you need to look settled.
- Whether you want to hear about a lip flip as well.

Consultations are free at both of our Knoxville-area locations, in Bearden and Farragut. The point of that meeting is not to sell you a syringe. It is to check whether what you wrote down matches what filler can actually do for your face, and to say so plainly if it does not.

# Checking clinic listings: a Knoxville guide to names, services and offices

*Names get shortened, suites get dropped and phones go stale. A practical way to check a local clinic listing against the practice's own website, with documented West Knoxville examples.*

By Sarah Hitchcox, RN

## Key Takeaways

- The name on a practice's own website can differ from a map listing, so compare both.
- More than one business can share a street address. The suite letter is what tells them apart.
- Read service focus from the practice's own service pages, not a directory category.
- The phone on a listing should belong to that specific office, not to a neighbor or a second location.
- The safest booking path is the page on the practice's own domain.

Booking a first appointment at a small West Knoxville clinic often starts with a listing that does not quite match the website. The name is slightly different, the address points to a building with several suites, and the directory phone may or may not ring at the right office. Practices grow, add offices and open sister brands, and listings catch up slowly.

Checking a listing takes a few minutes and saves a wasted drive or a call to the wrong front desk. The examples below come from three Knoxville businesses whose own websites document their names, services, suites and phone lines.

## Start with the exact name

The name on a practice's website is the one to trust. Directories and map apps often shorten it, add a city, or keep an older version. A listing for [Sarah Hitchcox Aesthetics](https://hitchcoxaesthetics.com), for example, should carry that full name. The home page and location pages use it consistently, and the owner, Sarah Hitchcox, RN, is named on the About page.

Trade names can also differ from what a site prints in its header. The [Botox Knox Med Spa](https://botoxknoxvilletn.com) website displays "Botox Knoxville TN" at the top of its pages, while its business listing uses the fuller name. Neither is wrong, but a reader comparing the two should expect that gap and confirm the address and phone rather than stopping at the name.

## Read the service focus from the practice's own pages

Directory categories are broad. "Med spa" says little about what a practice does day to day. The service pages on its own site are more specific and more current.

Sarah Hitchcox Aesthetics lists four service groups: injectables, laser services, microneedling and GLP-1 weight loss. Botox Knox Med Spa is narrower. Its pages focus on Botox, Dysport and Jeuveau for forehead lines, frown lines and crow's feet, along with lip flip and masseter treatments. [Knoxville Weight Loss Clinic](https://weightlossknoxvilletn.com) centers on physician-supervised weight loss with semaglutide and tirzepatide, with injectables, laser treatments and chemical peels listed as secondary services in its footer.

When a directory category and the service pages disagree, the service pages win.

## The suite letter matters more than the street

More than one business can share a street address, and the three businesses in this guide are an example. At 5113 Kingston Pike in Bearden, Sarah Hitchcox Aesthetics is in Suite 15. Botox Knox Med Spa lists Suite 15B and Knoxville Weight Loss Clinic lists Suite 15C at the same address. In Farragut, 102 S Campbell Station Road follows the same pattern: Suites 8, 8B and 8C.

Sarah Hitchcox Aesthetics also has two offices that its footer, which lists only Bearden and Farragut, would not reveal. Its location pages document all four:

- Bearden: 5113 Kingston Pike, Suite 15, Knoxville, TN 37919
- Farragut: 102 S Campbell Station Rd, Suite 8, Knoxville, TN 37934
- West Hills: 7600 Kingston Pike, #1550 Suite 30, Knoxville, TN 37919
- Cedar Bluff: 9141 Cross Park Dr, Suite 30, Knoxville, TN 37923

A listing that drops the suite, or copies a neighbor's, sends people to the wrong door.

## Match the phone to the office

A practice with several offices may publish a different phone for each one, and separate businesses in one building certainly do. The number on a listing should belong to the specific office listed.

For the four Sarah Hitchcox Aesthetics offices, the listing numbers are (865) 489-8008 for Bearden, West Hills and Cedar Bluff, and (865) 489-8001 for Farragut. Botox Knox Med Spa uses (865) 370-2246 in Bearden and (865) 370-2639 in Farragut. Knoxville Weight Loss Clinic uses (865) 500-3135 in Bearden and (865) 500-3510 in Farragut.

A listing that reuses one business's number for another at the same address, or shows a number matching none of the published lines, is worth a quick confirming call.

## Find the real booking destination

Not every clinic books the same way. Some use a scheduler on their own site, some prefer a call, and some use a contact form. A directory's "book now" button is not always the practice's own path.

All three businesses here publish a booking page on their own domain. Sarah Hitchcox Aesthetics labels it Book Online. Botox Knox Med Spa and Knoxville Weight Loss Clinic each label theirs Book Consultation. A listing that routes to a different scheduler, or to a form off the practice's domain, deserves a second look before anyone enters personal details.

The same principle applies to businesses managing their own presence. Quirko Hub's guide to [local service websites](https://www.quirkohub.com/local-service-websites-a-practical-content-plan/) makes the point that accurate, consistent information is what search tools and customers both rely on. A practice that keeps its name, suites, phones and booking path identical everywhere is far easier to verify.

## A short checklist before saving a listing

- Compare the name on the listing to the name on the practice's home page.
- Confirm the listing's category matches the practice's own service pages.
- Check the suite against the practice's location page, especially in shared buildings.
- Confirm the phone belongs to that office and not to a neighbor or a second location.
- Make sure the booking link lands on the practice's own domain.

## Conclusion

Clinic listings drift. Names get shortened, suites get dropped, phones go stale and booking links point to places the practice never chose. The practice's own website is the reference copy for all of it. Where three businesses share one address and differ only by a suite letter, a few minutes of checking is the difference between the right door and the hallway.

# Flights, Sun and Altitude: A Nurse's Rules for the Week Before a Trip

*A Knoxville nurse injector explains what a flight, a beach week and a mountain trip each do to your skin, and what she avoids in the days before leaving.*

By Sarah Hitchcox, RN

I am a nurse in Knoxville, and I spend a fair amount of my week talking to people about trips. Beach weeks in the fall. A work conference in Denver. A cabin in the Smokies for a long weekend. The question I hear is almost always the same: "Can I still come in before I leave?"

The honest answer is that it depends less on the treatment and more on the trip. A flight, a week of sun, and a few days at altitude each do something different to your skin and to your body. Once you know what each one does, the choices before you pack get much simpler.

This is how I think it through with my own patients. It is not a rulebook, and your own provider may see it differently. But it is what I actually do.

## Start with the trip, not the appointment

Most people plan backwards from a date on the calendar. They want to look rested for a wedding or a reunion, so they book the closest open slot before they fly.

I ask them to start somewhere else. What kind of trip is it? Will you be in the sun all day? Will you be somewhere dry and high? Will you be somewhere you cannot easily call me if something feels off?

Those three questions sort almost every trip I hear about into one of three buckets: the flight itself, the sun, and the altitude. Each bucket has its own short list of things I would rather you avoid in the days before you leave.

## What a flight does to you

Cabin air is dry. You sit still for hours. You lean your face against the window, or you fall asleep on your hand, or you rub your eyes when you land. None of that is dramatic on its own, but it is a poor environment for anything on your face that needs to be left alone.

Botox is the treatment people ask about most before a flight. At [Botox Knox Med Spa](https://botoxknoxvilletn.com), our West Knoxville injectables office, the appointment itself takes only ten to fifteen minutes and there is no downtime, so the plane is not really the concern. What I care about is timing. Botox does not do its full work the same day, and I would rather it be settled before you leave than settling somewhere I cannot see you.

So for a flight, my rule is simple. Do not make the injectable appointment the last thing you do before the airport. Give it room. If you have a question about how it looks or feels, I want you to be able to come back in, not send me a photo from a hotel bathroom.

Filler is a different conversation. It can swell for a few days, and a window seat with your cheek against the plastic is not where I want that swelling to happen. If a trip is close, I would rather talk about it in person than book it and hope.

On the plane itself, the things that help are not glamorous, and most of them are already in your bag. Water. A plain moisturizer you have used before. Sunscreen, even in a window seat, because the glass does not block all of it. Nothing new, nothing you have never put on your face.

## Sun: the beach, the lake, the boat

This is the bucket where I say no the most often, and it is almost always about lasers.

Laser hair removal, laser skin revitalization, and lesion reduction all work by putting energy into the skin. Sun does the same thing in its own way. Stacking the two close together is a bad idea, in either order. Freshly treated skin does not belong on a beach, and a fresh tan changes how I plan a laser session in the first place.

If you tell me you have a beach week coming up, I will usually hold off on laser and microneedling until you are back and the color has faded. That is not me being cautious for its own sake. It is the same conversation I would have with anyone who sits by a pool every weekend in July.

Sun is also why I ask about the trip at all. People sometimes book a laser series in the spring without mentioning that they spend every summer weekend on Norris Lake. The series does not fail. It just gets interrupted, and then we are picking it back up in October once the color has faded.

The same goes for a long weekend on a boat or an afternoon at a ballgame. It does not have to be a resort. If your skin is going to see a lot of sun, I want to know before I plan anything around it.

What travels well into the sun? Botox that has already settled. A sunscreen you like enough to reapply. A hat with a real brim. A moisturizer that does not sting. That is about it, and that is fine.

## Altitude: ski trips, mountain cabins, thin dry air

Altitude gets less attention than sun, but it combines two problems. The air is drier than at home, and the sun is stronger. A ski week is a beach week with a coat on.

There is a third problem that has nothing to do with skin. Mountain trips are often remote. A cabin an hour from a paved road is a wonderful place to be, and a bad place to be if you are wondering whether something is normal.

So for altitude, my rule is about newness. I do not want the week before a remote trip to be the first time you try anything. Not a first Botox appointment, not a first laser session, not a first round of a skincare product. Do the first time when you are home and can come back in. Do the repeat when you like, once you know how you respond.

That applies to our GLP-1 weight-loss program too. The medication is prescribed with regular check-ins, and dose changes happen at those visits. If you are traveling, say so at the check-in before you go. I would much rather plan around a trip than have a change land in the middle of it.

## The short list I avoid in the week before

If you take nothing else from this, take the list.

- **Anything for the first time.** New treatment, new product, new provider. The first time belongs at home.

# Planning Beauty Appointments Around a Trip: The Questions to Settle Before You Book

*A Knoxville nurse injector on lining up a trip and a treatment calendar without guessing: what to write down, what to ask your provider, and what the FDA and CDC say to pack.*

By Sarah Hitchcox, RN

I am a registered nurse in Knoxville, and the people who come to my practice are often managing two calendars at once. One is the trip. The other is the appointment they hoped to fit in before it: Botox, filler, a laser session, a microneedling visit, a weight-loss check-in, or the first consultation they have been meaning to book for months.

This article is not a set of clinical rules about how many days to leave between a treatment and a flight. Those answers depend on the treatment, the trip and the person, and the right place to get them is a consultation with your own provider. What I can do is lay out the planning work that makes that conversation short and useful: what to write down before you book, which questions to bring, and where the reliable public guidance on sun and medication lives.

## Start with the trip, not the appointment

Most people plan backwards from a date. They know when they leave, so they look for the closest open slot. That is understandable, but it puts the appointment in charge of the trip instead of the other way around.

Before you open a booking page, write down three things about the trip. The dates, including the day you leave and the day you are back. The kind of trip: a beach week, a ski cabin, a conference, a wedding weekend. And how reachable you will be. A resort with a pharmacy downstairs is a different situation from a cabin an hour from the nearest town.

None of those three points decides anything on its own. They are the facts your provider needs in order to give you a real answer instead of a general one. If you already keep a pre-trip list for the house, L'Essenziale's guide to the [essential home jobs to do before you travel](https://essenziale-hd.com/2025/10/17/essential-home-jobs-you-need-to-do-before-you-travel/) is the same idea applied to the kitchen and the garden. Add a line for appointments and you have one list instead of two.

## The questions worth asking before you book

This is the part I would rather you take from the article than any rule of thumb. Bring these questions to whoever is treating you, and expect an answer that is specific to the treatment you are booking.

- Does the timing of this appointment matter in relation to my departure date, and if so, which direction should I move it?
- Is there anything you would want me to avoid before or after the appointment, and does my trip include it?
- If something looks or feels different while I am away, how do I reach you, and what would you want to see or know?
- I will be in the sun most days. Does that change what you would recommend, or when?
- I am on a prescribed medication or injectable through your office. Does travel change how I take it, store it or carry it?
- Would you rather see me before the trip, after it, or both?

I am deliberately not answering those here. The answer for a fifteen-minute Botox appointment is not the answer for a laser series, and the answer for a beach week is not the answer for a conference. A provider who knows your skin, your history and your plan can answer in a sentence. A blog post cannot answer honestly for everyone.

## What a consultation is for

At [Sarah Hitchcox Aesthetics](https://hitchcoxaesthetics.com), consultations are free at our Bearden and Farragut offices, and they exist for exactly this kind of planning. The practice offers injectables, including Botox, fillers, SkinVive and Kybella; laser services for hair removal, skin revitalization, lesion reduction and skin tightening; microneedling; and medically supervised GLP-1 weight loss. Each of those has its own logistics, and a consultation is where the trip and the treatment get put on the same page.

A few practical facts from our own pages help with the calendar. A Botox appointment takes ten to fifteen minutes and has no downtime, so the visit itself is easy to fit into a full pre-trip week. A GLP-1 program is medically supervised, which means there is a schedule of visits behind it; if a trip falls near one of those, raise it rather than skip it. For laser services and microneedling, ask the sun question before you pick a date, and let the answer set the date.

## Sun: use the public guidance, then ask your own question

Sun protection on a trip is not really an aesthetics question, and you do not need my opinion on it. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration publishes plain [guidance on sunscreen](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/understanding-over-counter-medicines/sunscreen-how-help-protect-your-skin-sun): use a broad spectrum sunscreen with an SPF of 15 or higher, apply it about 15 minutes before going out, reapply at least every two hours and more often when swimming or sweating, and cover up with long sleeves, a broad-brimmed hat and sunglasses. The same page lists the spots people forget, including ears, lips, the back of the neck and the tops of the feet.

That is general advice for everyone. The specific question, whether your treatment plan changes anything about it, belongs to your provider. Ask it in the consultation and write the answer down next to your trip dates.

## Medications and paperwork: pack the way the CDC says

If you are on a prescribed medication or injectable, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's [Pack Smart checklist](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/travel/page/pack-smart) for travelers covers the paperwork side. It recommends carrying copies of your prescriptions, the prescriptions themselves preferably in their original containers, contact information for your healthcare professional at home, your health insurance documents, and a list of hospitals or clinics at your destination. It also points travelers to the Transportation Security Administration for which medicines and medical devices can be carried onto a plane, and notes that some countries restrict the medications you can bring in.

That checklist is the reason to ask your own provider the storage and carrying question before you leave. A prescription written for use at home may come with instructions that a hotel room, a checked bag or a border crossing complicates. Better to hear that in the office than to work it out at the airport.

## Choosing the office and getting the booking done

Location is the part of the plan people most often leave until the last minute. Sarah Hitchcox Aesthetics has four West Knoxville offices: Bearden at 5113 Kingston Pike, Suite 15; Farragut at 102 S. Campbell Station Road, Suite 8; West Hills at 7600 Kingston Pike, #1550, Suite 30; and Cedar Bluff at 9141 Cross Park Drive, Suite 30. Pick the one that sits on the route you actually drive in the week before a trip, not the one that looks closest on a map.

For wrinkle relaxers specifically, [Botox Knox Med Spa](https://botoxknoxvilletn.com) offers Botox, Dysport and Jeuveau from two West Knoxville locations: Bearden at 5113 Kingston Pike, Suite 15B, and Farragut at 102 S. Campbell Station Road, Suite 8B. Hours are Monday through Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., with Saturdays by appointment. The office books online with real-time availability and takes questions by text at each location's number. If your pre-trip week is already full, the Saturday-by-appointment line is the one to read twice.

Whichever office you choose, book the consultation first and the treatment second. Consultations are free at the Sarah Hitchcox Aesthetics Bearden and Farragut offices and complimentary at Botox Knox, and the consultation is the appointment where the trip gets discussed.

## A one-page plan you can actually use

Put these on the same sheet as your packing list:

- **Trip facts.** Departure and return dates, the type of trip, and how reachable you will be.
- **The questions above,** with space to write each answer next to it.
- **Sun plan.** The FDA basics, plus whatever your provider adds for your specific treatment.
- **Medication paperwork.** Copies of prescriptions, your provider's contact information, the CDC list, and any carrying or storage instructions from your own office.
- **Office and time.** Which location, which day, and whether the visit is before the trip, after it, or both.

When all five lines are filled in, the planning is done. The clinical decisions stay where they belong, with the person who has examined your skin and knows your history. That division of labor is what keeps a trip and a treatment from getting in each other's way, and it takes about twenty minutes at the kitchen table to set up.

# Before Your First Botox Visit: Turn Saved Photos Into Clear Questions

*You already have the screenshots. Here is how to turn them into questions a nurse can actually answer at a consultation.*

By Sarah Hitchcox, RN

## Start with the folder you already have

You probably have one. A folder of screenshots, a saved collection on Instagram, a photo of a friend from a wedding. Most people walk into a first Botox visit with pictures on their phone and no words to go with them.

That is not a problem. The pictures are useful. The work is turning them into questions.

At [Sarah Hitchcox Aesthetics](https://hitchcoxaesthetics.com/botox), I perform every Botox treatment myself, and the consultation before it is free at both of our Knoxville-area offices. The better your questions, the more we get out of that conversation.

## Sort the photos before you sort the words

Open the folder and split it into two piles. Not "want" and "don't want." Try these instead:

- Photos where you like a specific area: the forehead, the space between the brows, the corners of the eyes.
- Photos where you like the overall feeling but cannot point to a spot.

The first pile turns into questions quickly. The second pile is harder, and that is fine. "I like how rested she looks" is a starting point, not a dead end. What do you notice first when you look at that face? The brows? The eyes? Write that down.

## Learn the names for what you are pointing at

Botox is a neuromodulator. It temporarily blocks nerve signals to specific facial muscles so they do not contract as deeply, which softens the lines those muscles make. That is why treatment pages talk about areas, not whole faces.

Before your visit, read the treatment page for the practice you are considering and match your photos to its list. On mine, the areas listed are forehead lines, frown lines (the "11s" between the brows), crow's feet, bunny lines, chin dimpling, brow lift, gummy smile and lip flip.

Now go back to your photos. Is the thing you circled a forehead line or a frown line? Is it the brow position? Once you can name it, you can ask about it directly.

## Write three questions per photo

Keep it small. For each picture that made the cut, write:

1. What am I looking at? ("Her forehead is smooth but she can still raise her eyebrows.")
2. Is that a Botox area? (Check it against the list.)
3. What do I want to know about that area on my own face?

Bring the photos too. A consultation at my office includes assessing your muscle strength and facial anatomy, and a picture of what you like helps me explain what would translate to your face and what would not.

## Questions the treatment page raises on its own

Some questions come from reading, not from photos. A few worth adding:

- **Botox, Dysport or Jeuveau?** We carry more than one wrinkle relaxer and recommend based on your anatomy. Ask which one and why.
- **How long is the appointment?** Botox appointments with me take 10 to 15 minutes with no downtime. The consultation is a separate conversation, so plan for both.
- **Which office?** Bearden or Farragut for us. Write down the one you booked and the suite number.

If you are comparing more than one West Knoxville injector, [Botox Knox Med Spa](https://botoxknoxvilletn.com) lays out its Botox, Dysport and Jeuveau services the same way, with lip flip and masseter treatment listed by area, so the photo-to-list exercise works there too.

## Two things to leave in the folder

- A photo of someone else's face with the expectation of the same face. It is a description of a preference, not a plan.
- A list of questions copied from a comment thread. If you cannot say why you are asking, skip it.

## The one-page version

Before you leave for the appointment, you should have:

- The photos you kept, with the area named on each.
- Three questions per photo.
- Your product, timing and office questions.
- The name of the person you are meeting. At my practice, that is me, Sarah Hitchcox, RN.

Then close the folder. The photos got you to the questions. The conversation does the rest.

# What “Medically Supervised” Actually Means for GLP-1 Weight Loss

*A Knoxville nurse explains what supervision adds to a GLP-1 weight-loss program: labs, a dosing schedule, follow-ups, early side-effect care and who should not start.*

By Sarah Hitchcox, RN

Every ad for semaglutide or tirzepatide now carries the same two words: medically supervised. They appear on billboards, in telehealth pop-ups, and on the websites of clinics that have never met their patients in person. The phrase has become so common that it has stopped meaning anything, and that is a problem, because the difference between a supervised program and an unsupervised one is not a marketing detail. It is the whole thing.

I am a registered nurse. I spent most of my career in an emergency department before I opened my own practice in Knoxville, Tennessee, and I now run a GLP-1 weight-loss program alongside the aesthetic work I am better known for. This article is my attempt to explain, plainly, what supervision consists of. If you are thinking about these medications, you should be able to tell the real thing from the label.

## It starts with a conversation, not a form

Supervision begins before a prescription exists. A real consultation is a sit-down review of your health history: the conditions you have been diagnosed with, the medications you take, the surgeries you have had, and what you have already tried for your weight. It also covers why you want this now. Someone preparing for a knee replacement and someone who wants to lose fifteen pounds before a reunion are not the same patient, and the plan should not be the same either.

The consultation is also where the medication is chosen. Semaglutide and tirzepatide are both once-weekly injections, and both work by regulating appetite, slowing digestion, and changing how the body handles blood sugar. Tirzepatide acts on two hormone pathways rather than one. Which one fits you depends on your history and your goals, and that is a decision that should be made with you in the room, not by a default setting on an order form.

If a clinic asks for your weight and your card number and nothing else, that is a transaction. It is not supervision.

## Labs before the first dose

Baseline labs are the part of a program that is easiest to skip and hardest to justify skipping. The purpose is not to find a reason to say no. The purpose is to know where you are starting from, so that when something changes three months in, there is a number to compare it to.

What gets ordered depends on your history. In general terms, a baseline looks at how your blood sugar, kidneys and liver are doing, and sometimes at your thyroid. If you are already on medication for diabetes, that matters a great deal, because adding a GLP-1 on top of it changes the math on blood sugar and needs coordination with whoever prescribes the other medication.

Labs also do a quieter job. Sometimes they turn up something unrelated to weight that a person had no idea about. That is not a reason to fear them. It is the reason to have them.

## Who should not start

A good consultation sometimes ends with the words "not you, not now." That is not a failure of the visit. It is the visit working.

The prescribing information for these medications lists situations where they should not be used, and a supervised program asks about every one of them. They include:

- Pregnancy, plans to become pregnant soon, or breastfeeding.
- A personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer, or a condition called multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2.
- A history of pancreatitis.
- Certain stomach conditions that already slow digestion, since these medications slow it further.

There are also softer reasons to wait. A history of an eating disorder deserves a careful conversation. So does a life that is about to get chaotic in a way that makes weekly injections and regular visits unrealistic. None of these are judgments about the person. They are the reasons a nurse or physician exists in the process at all.

## Dosing is a schedule, not a number

People arrive asking what dose they will be on, as if it were a single fact. It is not. These medications are started low and stepped up over weeks, and the step-ups are supposed to happen on a schedule that is adjusted to how you tolerate each level. At my practice, the plan that comes out of a consultation includes the medication, the dosage schedule and nutrition guidance, because those three things are not separable.

The dose you end on is the one that works for you. It is not automatically the highest one on the chart. Some people do well at a middle step and stay there. Some need to move up slowly because their stomach objects at every increase. Supervision is the person who watches that and makes the call, rather than an autofill that bumps the dose every four weeks whether you are ready or not.

Missed doses come up constantly, and the right answer depends on how many days have passed and where you are in the schedule. That is exactly the kind of question you should be able to ask someone, and get an answer the same day.

## Side effects handled early, not endured

Nausea, constipation, a heavy full feeling after small meals, and tiredness are the common complaints, and they cluster around the first weeks on a new dose. Most of them are manageable. Smaller meals, more water, protein first, and slowing down the step-up schedule handle a great deal. Sometimes the right move is to hold at the current dose for an extra couple of weeks. Sometimes it is to step back down.

The point of supervision is that these adjustments happen early, when they are small. The people who struggle are the ones who push through a bad week alone because they do not want to bother anyone, or because there is no one to bother.

There are also symptoms that are not "push through" symptoms. Severe or persistent abdominal pain, vomiting that keeps you from holding down fluids, and signs of dehydration need a call the same day, and in some cases an emergency room. I spent years on the other side of that door. The patients who ended up there were almost never the ones who had someone to call at the first sign of trouble.

## Follow-ups are the program

Everything above is set up. The follow-ups are the program. A check-in is where weight, side effects, food, and the next dose decision all get looked at together, and it is where the schedule actually gets adjusted. In the early months they should be frequent. Later, once you are stable on a dose, they can spread out, but they should not disappear.

Medication alone is not enough, and I say that as someone who prescribes it. The appetite change is a window, and what you eat during that window decides whether you keep muscle or lose it along with fat. Nutrition guidance is part of a supervised plan for that reason, not as an add-on.

Follow-ups are also where the honest conversations about plateaus and stopping happen. Weight loss on these medications is not a straight line, and a stall is a normal part of the course rather than a sign that something is broken. Eventually, the question of how long to continue and what maintenance looks like has to be answered too. That is not a conversation you can have with a refill button.

## What it looks like at my practice

I run two offices in the Knoxville area, one in Bearden and one in Farragut. Our [GLP-1 weight-loss program](https://hitchcoxaesthetics.com/weight-loss) offers semaglutide and tirzepatide, and every patient starts with a consultation that covers medical history and goals before a personalized plan is written. Regular check-ins, dose adjustments and lifestyle coaching are built into the program rather than sold separately. I am currently working toward my Doctor of Nursing Practice, and the emergency-department years still shape how I think about this work: the goal is never to have anyone find out the hard way that a question went unasked.

## The short version

Supervision is not a phrase. It is a set of things that either happen or do not:

- A consultation that reviews your history before anything is prescribed.
- Baseline labs, with someone who reads them.
- A clear answer on whether you are a candidate, including when the answer is no.
- A dosing schedule that responds to how you are doing.
- Side effects addressed in the first week, not the fourth.
- Follow-ups that continue for as long as the medication does.

Ask any clinic which of these they do, and who does it. If the answer is vague, the two words on the ad were doing more work than the clinic is.

# Dermal Fillers: The Safety Conversation to Have Before You Book

*A nurse injector on the questions about anatomy, reversibility and aftercare that belong in your consultation, not in your search history afterwards.*

By Sarah Hitchcox, RN

Most people who ask me about dermal fillers have already decided what they want. Fuller lips, softer cheeks, a smoother line from the nose to the mouth. What they have usually not decided is what they want to know before someone puts a needle near their face.

I am a registered nurse in Knoxville, Tennessee, and I spent most of my nursing career in the emergency department before moving into aesthetics. That background shapes how I talk about fillers. The result matters, but the conversation about safety comes first, and it should happen before you book, not in the chair.

Here is what I think that conversation should cover.

## Start with what filler is

Most of the fillers used in the face today are made from hyaluronic acid, a sugar molecule your body already makes. At [Sarah Hitchcox Aesthetics](https://hitchcoxaesthetics.com) we use hyaluronic acid fillers to restore volume and add definition to areas like the cheeks and lips.

The gel is placed under the skin in small amounts. It adds volume where volume has been lost, or shape where you want more of it. It is not a wrinkle relaxer. Botox and similar products work on muscles. Filler works on structure.

That difference matters. It tells you what a filler can and cannot do, and it explains why the safety questions are different from the ones you would ask about Botox.

## Ask about anatomy, not just areas

The face is not a flat surface. Under the skin there are arteries, veins and nerves, and their paths vary from one person to the next. A good injector is not thinking about "the lips" or "the cheeks." They are thinking about where the vessels run in your face and how deep the product should go.

The most serious filler complication is product entering or pressing on a blood vessel. It is uncommon, but it is the reason the training and anatomy knowledge of your injector matter more than the brand of filler.

So ask directly. What is your training? What license do you hold? How do you plan the injection around the vessels in this area? An injector who welcomes those questions is telling you something. One who brushes them off is telling you something too.

## Some areas call for more caution

Not every part of the face carries the same risk. Lips and cheeks are the areas people ask me about most. Other areas, such as the nose, the space between the eyebrows and the skin under the eyes, sit close to important vessels and need a more careful conversation.

That does not mean those areas are off limits. It means the injector should be able to explain what makes them different, why they might use less product or a different technique, and when they would say no. I would rather tell someone an area is not a good fit than take the risk.

If you have had filler before, tell your injector where and when. Older product can still be present months later, and it changes how a new treatment is planned.

## Reversibility is a real advantage

One reason hyaluronic acid fillers are used so widely is that they can be dissolved. An enzyme called hyaluronidase breaks the gel down. It is used in an emergency if filler is affecting blood flow, and it can also be used when a result is simply not right.

Before you book, ask whether the provider keeps hyaluronidase on hand and has used it. This is not a hypothetical. It is the safety net, and you want to know it exists in the room where you are being treated.

Not every filler is reversible. Some products work by stimulating collagen and cannot be dissolved. If someone suggests one of those, ask why it is being chosen over a hyaluronic acid filler and what happens if you do not like the outcome.

## Where you are treated matters

Filler is a medical procedure and belongs in a medical setting, with a licensed provider who can recognize a problem and manage it. In my practice, treatment happens in our Bearden and Farragut offices, and we offer a free consultation first so the safety conversation is not squeezed into the treatment appointment.

If you are looking in West Knoxville, [Botox Knox Med Spa](https://botoxknoxvilletn.com) lists on its site the things I tell people to look for: FDA-approved products, board-certified providers and a stated focus on natural results, for Botox, Dysport and Jeuveau as well as lip filler. Wherever you go, look for the same.

## Aftercare is part of safety

The first day or two after filler is when problems show up, so aftercare is not only about protecting the result. Some swelling and bruising are expected. Increasing pain, skin that turns pale or blotchy, or any change in your vision is not, and you should call your provider right away.

Before you leave the appointment, you should know how to reach your injector after hours. If a practice cannot tell you that, book somewhere else.

## The short version

If you take one thing from this, take the questions. Who is injecting me, and what is their training? Which product, and can it be dissolved? Is the reversal enzyme on site? What makes this area more or less risky? How do I reach you if something feels wrong?

A consultation that answers all five is a good sign. You may still decide filler is not for you, and that is a fine outcome too. The point is to decide with the safety conversation behind you, not ahead of you.
